title: Martin Lawrence Live: Runteldat
full_review:
Apparently fed up with all the lies and gossip spread about him, comedian Martin Lawrence decides to tell his side of the story regarding his troubles and woes in recent years in the vulgar film "Martin Lawrence Live: Runteldat" (Paramount).

But the movie is actually just two hours of Lawrence blathering on in the most depraved manner about sex and relationships. Filmed by director David Raynr in front of a live audience, Lawrence's every other word is either an expletive or a filthy phrase of some sort. The live audience seems to find his antics and potty mouth hysterically funny. But most of it seems to be laughter induced by the shocking things he spouts rather than by anything genuinely funny or observant.

The film begins with a short documentary-style segment, narrated by Lawrence, which chronicles his triumphs and tribulations of the past few years. As young man who found superstardom with a hit TV series, Lawrence suddenly falls prey to the usual Hollywood temptations: drugs and alcohol. Not so long after being arrested on drug charges, Lawrence collapses from heat stroke and slips into a coma for three days. In his opening words, he promises to address these issues as they really happened, not as they were sensationalized by the media. But it's not until nearly the end of the show that he does, and he makes no astounding revelations about his actions. He really was hopped up on drugs when they arrested him. And the disgusting explanation about his bowel functions in the hospital after his heat stroke is repulsive and completely unfunny. It's pointless gross-out comedy at its lowest.

The worst part of his shtick is his objectification of men and women as sexual toys for one another. He talks of "inspecting" certain body parts before committing to one another. It's all crass and aimed at the lowest common denominator. He's also includes several racist comments about Arabs, as if the Sept. 11 attack is an excuse to bash Middle Easterners.

Surprisingly, throughout his act, Lawrence gives thanks to God, crediting him with "bringing him back" from the brink of destruction. He seems genuine in his sentiments here, but almost before his last words of thanksgiving are out, he has already moved on to more base and depraved commentary.

There may be some who find his performance entertaining, but the vast majority of moviegoers are likely to write this off as a bawdy exercise of self aggrandizement.

Due to explicit and denigrating sexual dialogue with nonstop rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
(
2002
)
